name: May 2024 Gannon Superstorm

phenomena.details: Multiple X-class flares from AR 13664 between May 8–11; largest was X5.8 on May 11. X1.0 on May 8, X2.2 on May 9, X3.9 on May 10.
Multiple CMEs in quick succession from AR 13664 beginning May 8; CME sequence arrived May 10–11. Fastest estimated at ~1700 km/s.
G5 extreme geomagnetic storm – first since October 2003. Peak Dst −412 nT, Kp 9 on May 10–11.
Moderate SEP event associated with the flare complex.

impacts.description: Aurora visible worldwide at historically low latitudes: Florida (~27°N), Texas, southern Spain, northern Mexico, Okinawa (Japan, ~26°N), Caribbean islands. The most widespread global aurora display since October 2003; social media amplified the phenomenon to millions of observers.

GPS/GNSS positioning errors of 10–100+ m reported across North America, Europe, and Asia during storm peak; USDA NRCS documented agricultural GPS system failures across the US Midwest during spring planting season.

Starlink experienced enhanced atmospheric drag due to thermospheric heating and expansion; dozens of satellites required orbit maintenance maneuvers. Satellite operators across the industry reported elevated conjunction warnings from altitude degradation.

GIC events detected in power grids across North America and Europe; transformer saturation effects reported in several countries. No major grid failures, but several utilities activated GIC protection measures.

papers.title: The Gannon Superstorm of May 2024: Observations, impacts, and implications for space weather preparedness
papers.authors: Hayakawa, H., Oliveira, D. M., Guerrero, J. M., et al.
papers.keyFinding: Comprehensive characterization of the May 2024 G5 storm, confirming Dst −412 nT, worldwide aurora to within 25° of the equator, and extensive GPS disruption – the first G5 event since Halloween 2003.

summary: The May 2024 Gannon Superstorm – the first G5 geomagnetic storm since 2003 – sent aurora dancing across the skies of Florida, Mexico, and Japan at latitudes near 25°, while disabling GPS systems during spring planting season and stressing satellite orbits, demonstrating Solar Cycle 25's surprising vigor.
description: Active region AR 13664, one of the most productive of Solar Cycle 25's ascending phase, began erupting on May 8, 2024, producing a rapid sequence of X-class flares and CMEs over four days. The compound CME arrival on May 10–11 drove a G5 extreme geomagnetic storm – the first since the Halloween Storms of October 2003 – with a peak Dst of −412 nT and Kp 9. The southward component of the interplanetary magnetic field (Bz) reached −68 nT. Aurora was visible to the naked eye at geographic latitudes as low as ~25°N across North America, Europe, and Asia, including from Florida, Texas, northern Mexico, southern Spain, and Japan. Social media delivered the aurora display to a global audience as never before. The GPS/GNSS community documented widespread positioning errors of 10–100+ m, affecting agriculture (spring planting), aviation, and emergency services. The storm was informally named the 'Gannon Superstorm' in recognition of space weather scientist Jennifer Gannon. Solar Cycle 25, which had been forecast in 2019 to be weak, was by this point tracking well above predictions – raising new questions about solar cycle forecasting.
